title: The Complete Japan Travel Guide
subtitle: How the regions divide, why the shinkansen rewards planning, and what a fortnight can honestly cover.
summary: Japan packs ultra-modern cities, centuries-old temples, volcanic mountains and subtropical islands into a country the shinkansen network makes easy to combine. This guide covers how the regions differ, when a JR Pass actually pays for itself, what the seasons really mean from cherry blossoms to autumn foliage, and the practicalities — cash culture and etiquette — that catch first-time visitors out most often.

sections.title: How Japan divides
body: Japan stretches over 3,000 kilometres from subtropical Okinawa to snowbound Hokkaido, and treating it as a single climate or single culture is the most common mistake first-time visitors make in planning.
**Tokyo and the east.** [[tokyo|Tokyo]] itself, a genuine world city of dense neighbourhoods and technological energy, and [[nikko|Nikko]], an easy mountain day trip of elaborate shrines and forest.

**Kansai and the historic heartland.** [[kyoto|Kyoto]] for temples, geisha districts and imperial history, [[osaka-nara|Osaka and Nara]] for street food and Japan's first permanent capital's deer park and temples.
**Western Japan.** [[hiroshima-miyajima|Hiroshima and Miyajima]], a city rebuilt around a direct reckoning with its history, beside an island shrine considered one of the country's most scenic views.

**The mountains.** [[mount-fuji-hakone|Mount Fuji and Hakone]] for the country's defining volcano and its onsen towns, and [[takayama-shirakawa-go|Takayama and Shirakawa-go]] plus [[kanazawa|Kanazawa]] for the Japanese Alps' preserved old towns and thatched-roof villages.

**The far north and south.** [[hokkaido|Hokkaido]], wilderness, snow and a distinct food culture, and [[okinawa|Okinawa]], subtropical islands and coral reefs that feel like a different country entirely.
sections.note: The practical unit for a first trip is Tokyo plus Kansai, not an attempt at the whole country. The shinkansen makes the Tokyo-Kyoto-Osaka-Hiroshima corridor easy; Hokkaido and Okinawa each reward dedicated time of their own.

list.title: If this is your first trip
list.text: [[tokyo]], [[kyoto]] and [[osaka-nara]], connected by shinkansen. Four nights in Tokyo, three in Kyoto, two in Osaka with a Nara day trip. It is the standard Golden Route because it works: a modern capital, historic temples and Japan's best street food, no car required.

list.title: If you want mountains and hot springs
list.text: [[mount-fuji-hakone|Mount Fuji and Hakone]] for volcanic scenery, ryokan inns and onsen bathing — rewards one or two nights and pairs naturally as a stop between Tokyo and Kyoto.

list.title: If you want history and a direct reckoning with the past
list.text: [[hiroshima-miyajima|Hiroshima and Miyajima]], the Peace Memorial Park and Museum beside one of Japan's most photographed shrine views, an easy shinkansen extension from Osaka or Kyoto.

list.title: If you want preserved old towns without the crowds
list.text: [[takayama-shirakawa-go|Takayama and Shirakawa-go]] for a mountain merchant town and thatched-roof farmhouse village, or [[kanazawa|Kanazawa]] for an underrated castle town with one of Japan's great gardens.

list.title: If you want wilderness or islands
list.text: [[hokkaido|Hokkaido]] for mountains, snow and seafood in the north, or [[okinawa|Okinawa]] for coral reefs and a distinct island culture in the south, both a short flight from Tokyo or Osaka.

list.title: If you want something different from the classic route
list.text: [[nikko|Nikko]] for elaborate shrines and forest an easy day trip from Tokyo, most first-time Japan visitors never reach it despite the short journey.

sections.title: Getting around: the shinkansen, JR Pass and one common mistake
body: Japan's rail network is excellent, used correctly. [[tokyo|Tokyo]] to [[kyoto|Kyoto]] is about 2h15 on the shinkansen, [[osaka-nara|Osaka]] to [[hiroshima-miyajima|Hiroshima]] under 2 hours.

**Run the numbers on a JR Pass before buying.** It can offer real savings on a long, multi-city itinerary, but for a shorter or more Tokyo-focused trip, individual tickets sometimes work out cheaper — price your specific route both ways before committing.

**Get an IC card on arrival.** Suica or Pasmo cover nearly all local trains, buses and many convenience store purchases nationwide on a single tap-in, tap-out card, and now work well alongside a JR Pass for local hops it doesn't cover.

**A car is useful** for [[hokkaido|Hokkaido's]] wider distances and reaching [[takayama-shirakawa-go|Shirakawa-go's]] rural villages comfortably. Hire it only for that specific leg — a car in Tokyo, Kyoto or Osaka is expensive and actively unhelpful.

**Domestic flights** are the practical way to reach [[hokkaido|Hokkaido]] and [[okinawa|Okinawa]] quickly, both a considerable rail or ferry journey from Tokyo otherwise — budget carriers like Peach offer low fares booked a little ahead.
**Reserved seats are usually free** with rail passes and worth booking a day or two ahead in peak season, particularly around cherry blossom time.
sections.note: Buy a JR Pass, if it suits your route, before you leave home — it is generally more expensive or unavailable once purchased inside Japan.

sections.title: When to go
body: Japan's climate varies significantly by latitude, which makes 'the best time' as much about the country's two signature natural seasons as about guaranteed sunshine. Two windows generally work best: **late March to May** and **October to November**.
**Spring** brings cherry blossom season, worth planning specific dates around, though forecasts shift year to year and popular spots get crowded — book accommodation well ahead.
**Summer** is hot, humid and prone to a June rainy season across most of the country, though it is also festival season and the best time to escape north to Hokkaido's pleasant cooler climate.

**Autumn**, especially November, brings koyo foliage that arguably rivals spring blossoms for spectacle and draws slightly smaller crowds — an excellent window for photography and comfortable walking weather.
**Winter** is cold but clear across most of the country, with excellent skiing in Hokkaido and the Japanese Alps, and Japan's onsen culture comes into its own against a snowy backdrop.
sections.note: Golden Week (late April into early May) and Obon (mid-August) see domestic travel surge nationwide — book well ahead or plan around these windows if you can.

sections.title: Costs, cash culture and what you must book
body: Mid-range travel in Japan runs roughly **¥15,000–25,000 per person per day**, with [[tokyo|Tokyo]] accommodation adding a modest 15–20% premium over that figure. Backpacking works at ¥7,000–11,000; comfortable travel with good hotels or ryokan and first-class rail runs ¥30,000–55,000.

**Carry cash.** Japan remains more cash-reliant than its technological reputation suggests — card and contactless coverage has expanded considerably, but smaller restaurants and shops, especially outside major cities, are still often cash-only.
**Convenience stores are a genuine budget ally**, not just a last resort — onigiri, sandwiches and hot food from 7-Eleven, Lawson or FamilyMart hold up as legitimately good, cheap meals at any hour.

**Book ahead, without exception:** a JR Pass if your route suits one, popular restaurants and teamLab-style attractions in Tokyo, and any accommodation during cherry blossom season, Golden Week or Obon.

**Small savings that add up:** standing ramen counters and conveyor-belt sushi over tourist-district restaurants, convenience store breakfasts over hotel ones, and an IC card to avoid single-ticket fare calculations on every local trip.

sections.title: Culture, quiet trains and how onsen bathing works
body: Japanese culture varies by region, but a handful of broadly shared norms hold nationwide, and a little preparation goes a long way toward feeling less like a visible outsider.
**Shoes come off indoors, without exception.** Homes, many restaurants, ryokan inns and some temples require shoes removed at the entrance — watch for a raised floor or shoe rack as the signal.
**Trains are kept quiet.** Phone calls are considered inconsiderate, and most passengers keep conversation low — step between cars if a call is unavoidable.
**Tipping is not customary**, and can cause genuine confusion if offered. Good service is the built-in standard rather than something rewarded separately.
**Queuing is taken seriously** — orderly lines for trains, elevators and shops are a genuine social expectation, and cutting in is noticed.

Finally, take **onsen etiquette** seriously: wash thoroughly at the seated shower stations before entering the shared bath, and check policies on tattoos ahead, since some traditional bathhouses still restrict them.

list.title: Ten days: the classic Golden Route
list.text: Four nights in [[tokyo]], three in [[kyoto|Kyoto]] with a [[osaka-nara|Nara]] day trip, three in [[osaka-nara|Osaka]], all by shinkansen. The most trodden route in Japan and still the right first trip — a modern capital, historic temples and the country's best street food, no car needed.
list.tip: Book teamLab-style Tokyo attractions and any cherry blossom season accommodation before you leave home — both sell out or spike in price close to the date.

list.title: Two weeks: cities and history
list.text: The itinerary on the [[c:japan|Japan country page]]: [[tokyo]], [[nikko|Nikko]], [[kyoto]], [[osaka-nara|Nara]], [[osaka-nara|Osaka]] and [[hiroshima-miyajima|Hiroshima]]. Adds a mountain shrine day trip and a direct reckoning with 20th-century history to the classic cities route.
list.tip: Buy shinkansen reserved seats a day or two ahead once your dates are fixed — walk-up availability tightens considerably in peak season.

list.title: Ten days in the mountains
list.text: [[tokyo]] for three nights, then [[mount-fuji-hakone|Mount Fuji and Hakone]], [[takayama-shirakawa-go|Takayama and Shirakawa-go]] and [[kanazawa|Kanazawa]] for a week. Slower and far more rural than the classic Golden Route.
list.tip: A rental car for the Takayama-Shirakawa-go-Kanazawa leg is worth it — bus connections exist but run infrequently.

list.title: A week in one region
list.text: [[hokkaido|Hokkaido]] as a self-contained northern trip of mountains and seafood, or [[okinawa|Okinawa]] for a subtropical island week of coral reefs and a distinct culture. Both reward a full week and neither works well as a rushed add-on to Tokyo.
list.tip: Book a domestic flight rather than attempting the long rail or ferry journey to either region unless the journey itself is the point.

faq.q: How long do I need in Japan?
faq.a: Ten to fourteen days for a first trip. Eight to ten covers Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka properly by shinkansen; twelve to sixteen lets you add Nikko and Hiroshima, which is the itinerary on this page. Five or six days is enough for Tokyo alone, and Tokyo alone justifies a trip.

faq.q: Should I buy a JR Pass?
faq.a: Only if your specific route benefits from it — price individual shinkansen tickets for your planned journeys and compare before buying. It pays off well on a long, multi-city itinerary but not always on a shorter or more Tokyo-focused trip.

faq.q: What is the single most common mistake visitors make?
faq.a: Not pricing the JR Pass against individual tickets for their actual route, and buying one reflexively. The second most common: underestimating how cash-reliant Japan still is outside major tourist areas.

Nowhere is truly a bad time, but Golden Week in late April into early May and Obon in mid-August see domestic travel surge nationwide, pushing prices up and availability down unless you book well ahead.
